newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to use paid informants in Ruiz Massieu trial.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to use paid informants in Ruiz Massieu trial.

text.p: U.S. prosecutors said in court papers filed on Friday they intend to use paid informants and convicted felons seeking sentence reductions to testify in a civil trial against a former Mexican deputy attorney general accused of taking bribes from drug-traffickers.

The disclosure came in a flurry of eleventh-hour motions filed in federal court ahead of Monday's trial in which the U.S. government will try to seize a $9 million Houston bank account held by Mario Ruiz Massieu.

Prosecutors say Ruiz Massieu, once a top drug-fighter in the Mexican attorney general's office, received the money from drug-traffickers seeking protection. He has argued that it was family money placed in the United States for safekeeping.

Prosecutors said in court documents they plan to call witnesses from U.S. law enforcement agencies to testify in the case and also will likely use "confidential informants, persons who are paid for their assistance."

"It is also anticipated during trial of this case that ... persons previously convicted of federal crimes ... will testify. In such instances, cooperation is given in exchange for a possible reduction in their federal sentence," said a motion by the government giving U.S. District Judge Nancy Atlas questions for potential jurors.

The names of the possible witnesses were not disclosed. In an earlier affidavit defence attorney Tony Canales said one government informant told authorities he twice delivered protection money to Ruiz Massieu in meetings that were either attended or arranged by Raul Salinas de Gortari, the jailed brother of former Mexican President Carlos Salinas de Gortari.

As a result, Canales asked for and got permission to question Raul Salinas on videotape for a possible showing at the trial. In an order filed on Wednesday, Atlas asked the Mexican government for assistance in setting up the deposition hearing, but the response was not known.

Canales' affidavit said Salinas would testify that the government informant had lied. Salinas has been in jail in Mexico City for two years without trial on charges he amassed an illegal fortune and masterminded the September 1994 assassination of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, a Mexico ruling party leader and brother of Mario Ruiz Massieu.

According to earlier news reports, another government informant said Salinas and Ruiz Massieu were part of a ring of Mexican officials who took millions of dollars in bribes from drug-traffickers. The ring was said to be led by Raul Salinas Lozano, the father of the Salinas brothers, but the family has denied the allegations.
News reports said prosecutors have evidence linking Ruiz Massieu to drug traffickers including convicted kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego and Amado Carrillo Fuentes.
